Virility is a noun that refers to the qualities, characteristics, and powers that are traditionally associated with being a fully developed, capable, and strong adult male. Think of it as the full package of what society has historically considered "ideal manliness" — physical strength, sexual power, energy, and forcefulness — all bundled into a single word.

If someone says a man "possesses great virility," they mean he embodies masculine power in a strong, noticeable way.
The Two Layers of Its Meaning

The word operates on two levels simultaneously, and understanding both is key.

The first layer is biological and sexual. At its most specific, virility refers to a male's sexual potency — his capacity to perform sexually and, in a broader biological sense, his reproductive capability. This is the most precise, literal use of the word. When doctors, biologists, or health writers use it, they usually mean it in this sense. A man is said to have virility when his body functions with full male sexual capability. When that ability declines — due to age, illness, or stress — people often say his virility has diminished.

The second layer is broader and more social. Beyond the bedroom, virility also describes a cluster of traits that cultures have long associated with powerful, vigorous manhood: physical strength, boldness, assertiveness, stamina, dominance, and raw energy. In this sense, a man chopping wood with ease, commanding a room with confidence, or leading others with decisive authority might all be described as displaying virility. It is the impression of masculine vitality in full bloom.

These two layers are deeply connected. Historically, societies linked a man's sexual power to his overall strength and dominance, which is why one word covers both.

Virility is not the same as fertility, though the two are related. Fertility is specifically about the ability to reproduce — producing healthy sperm that can result in a child. Virility is bigger than that. A man can be described as virile based on his physical presence, energy, and strength even in conversations that have nothing to do with reproduction.

Virility is also not a synonym for maturity or wisdom. A very old, wise man would not typically be called virile. The word carries an undertone of active, physical, energetic power — it leans young and vigorous rather than calm and experienced.
The Feeling and Weight of the Word

Virility is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries real cultural and emotional weight. It suggests something impressive, even admirable in a traditional sense. When someone uses it, there is often an undertone of admiration or longing attached — either appreciating its presence or mourning its absence.

This is why the word shows up so often in:

Advertising — cars, cologne, gym supplements, and health products are frequently marketed using the idea of virility because they promise to enhance or restore these masculine qualities.

Literature and poetry — writers use it to describe powerful, forceful characters, or even to describe the raw energy of nature itself. A stormy sea, a roaring fire, or a great lion might metaphorically be called virile, meaning they radiate an untamed, commanding power.

Medical and psychological discussions — particularly around aging, where the gradual decline of testosterone and physical capability is often framed as a loss of virility, something many men feel deeply about.

Certain things in culture become "symbols of virility" — objects, behaviors, or achievements that people associate with masculine power. A sports car, a muscular physique, a military uniform, or even the ability to grow a thick beard have, at various points in history or in various cultures, been treated as outward signs of a man's virility. This shows just how deeply the idea runs — it is not just about what is inside a man biologically, but about what he projects to the world.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are natural examples that show the word in both its layers:

"He was in his forties, but his energy and confidence radiated a kind of virility that made people take notice."

"The advertisement implied that drinking their protein shake would restore a man's lost virility."

"Some cultures tie a man's sense of identity so tightly to virility that any physical weakness feels like a personal failure."

"The sculptor carved the figure with broad shoulders and a commanding posture — every detail was meant to project virility."

"After his illness, he struggled not just with his health but with a feeling that his virility had been taken from him."

It is worth knowing that in modern times, the concept of virility is sometimes discussed critically. Scholars, feminists, and psychologists point out that when societies place enormous value on virility, they can create unhealthy pressure on men — pushing them to suppress vulnerability, avoid asking for help, and measure their worth through physical dominance or sexual performance. The idea of proving one's virility has, in many cases, led men to take unnecessary risks or feel shame about completely normal changes in their bodies as they age.

So while the word itself is simply descriptive, the cultural idea it represents is an active topic of conversation about what it means to be a man, how those expectations affect men's mental health, and whether those traditional definitions of manliness still serve people well today.

If you had to remember just one thing: virility is the noun for the full, vigorous expression of male power — covering sexual potency, physical strength, and bold masculine energy — and it carries deep cultural significance about what society considers ideal manhood.
